newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain's Co-op Bank hits new profit high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain's Co-op Bank hits new profit high.

text.p: Britain's Co-operative Bank Plc on Wednesday reported its third successive year of record profits and reiterated that it is not up for sale.

"The board and our parent company's board have said that our company is not for sale," managing director Terry Thomas told Reuters when asked about a recent approach by Lanica Trust to the bank's owner the Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS).
Earlier the bank announced that annual pretax profits rose by 24 percent to 45.5 million pounds ($75 million) for the year to January 11, 1997.

Known for its ethical and environmental stance, the smallest of Britain's clearing banks has only three percent of the market but has successfully targeted higher earning customers by introducing telephone banking and other innovations.

It hit the headlines in February when entrepreneur Andrew Regan's Lanica Trust made an approach to the CWS "to discuss the possible puchase of certain non-food businesses". These range from insurance to funeral parlours and travel agencies.

Thomas said that if Regan had asked the Bank of England to rule that he would be fit and proper person to run the Co-op as had been reported in the British press, he did not expect such approval to be given.

"It just isn't going to happen," he said, adding that Regan had no track record in banking and the BoE would be asking some "pretty searching questions". He said he suspected Regan's real target was not the Co-op Bank but the Co-operative Insurance Society.

Thomas has received around 800 letters from customers who did not want the bank to be sold and has seen no evidence of so-called "carpet-baggers" opening accounts in anticipation of a pay-back in the event of a successful takeover.
Shares in Lanica, which were star performers last year on speculation over Regan's intentions, were suspended on February 10 at 19.50 pounds each.

Thomas said he looked forward "with great interest" to the time when trading resumed. Stressing that his opinion was purely from a banker's advisory point of view, he said he expected they would "drop like a stone".
The bank said retail deposits were now double their level five years ago, retail lending has risen 16 percent and total assets had risen to 4.5 billion pounds.
"We are capturing more market share," said Thomas, who retires from the bank later this year.
He said nothing should be read into a proposed increase in the Co-op's share capital, which was agreed by the CWS before the emergence of the Regan attempt to buy its non-food businesses.

By reinvesting five million pounds in the bank's capital, it was indicating it regarded it as a core business and the increase was a prudent step needed to ensure the bank was not restricted in its growth, which was expected to continue to be strong.
Thomas said the Co-op, which has expanded in recent years, was not complacent and was investing heavily so it could compete in the next century, even if this meant a higher cost-income ratio.

He said that 50 percent of its branches had already converted to fully-automated operations which were open 24 hours a day and by the end of 1999 all its branches would have made the transition, although staff would not be laid off as a result.

Changes in banking, with increasing automation, were being addressed by the Co-op ahead of its larger rivals. This would prove to be a major problem as they would either have to reduce staff on a large scale, cut back branches or charge their customers more.

Such charges could be imposed by Britain's high street banks by 2000 if they did not reduce staff. Thomas said the Co-op would close 10 traditional branches during 1997 and replace them with more up-to-date modern branches.
And a number of breweries had already expressed interest in buying the old sites, which Thomas described as "mausoleums", many of them prime sites.

The Co-op's provisions for bad and doubtful debts in the year ended January 11 1997 rose to 23.7 million pounds from 22.7 million in 1995 but represented only 1.2 percent of average retail balances compared with 1.4 percent the year before.
